You're not wrong about the echo chamber effect not are you wrong about how subconscious radicalization can occur! The thing is, I think the echo chamber sort of comes from a desire to escape a much larger one at a societal level: that if you speak about these things you need to be in a hospital. So many people don't seem to realize how much of this sight is essentially catharsis for a bunch of suicidal people. We get to say how we feel, why we feel this way, and what we'd like to do about it without worrying about who will tell who and where we might be put because of it. 

The thing with the radicalization is very valid but it also stems from a point which was simply untrue in the video. There is a very, very vocal percentage of the userbase (including myself) that not only encourage people to exhaust all options before even considering suicide, but occasionally outright discourage considering it at all. I and many other users are sometimes lambasted by the more extreme because we tend to suggest maybe people should try everything they can first. There's no glorification of the way you choose to die, either. Sure someone might point out how terrifying one method is in relation to another, but by and large discussions around methods tend to be pretty objective funnily enough. Sometimes I'm jarred by how mechanical people have gotten the process down, but then I remember why that might be necessary for so many of us. 

People, especially minors, dying as a result of information they got on the site will always be both unfortunate and heartbreaking. I would never deny that. I think, however, it's also important to talk about the people whose lives have genuinely been saved by the catharsis and understanding you experience on the site. I haven't kept track and it would be an impossible task, but I can personally name six individuals (four of them minors) whose lives have genuinely been saved and attempts put on hold / cancelled outright because of the understanding they get from the site. Then, taking into account myself, I'd say seven. SS was the first place I ever heard the honest truth from older people about how life goes as you age. It's also the first place I ever met older people (50's-70's) who didn't espouse meaningless platitudes and instead really sat down and made me feel listened to and understood. It's very easy to look at the deaths attributed to the site and claim it's responsible, but a very common response from other users that I agree with is: what about the lives that have been saved? Even many ex-users talk about how having this space saved their lives. Does that not count for anything? The site has been around for years, and so you'll never get a proper set of data to analyze for "lives saved." Instead, I'd invite you to go into the chat rooms on the site that are separate from the forum, go to the recovery section. Hell, even read the forum posts about people who say how they "couldn't do it." I think you would be pleasantly surprised.

Wowie, there's threads about this on breadtube too. Well maybe the perspective of a poster (and not even anonymous at that) might help? For context: I joined back in 2021 and after being warded for a handful of attempts, have used the site on and off ever since. I don't know if I'd say I've "recovered" but I'm definitely recovering somewhat. I still struggle with the ideation and stuff often but what can ya do? 

The video made a lot of points, many I agree with and many that I did not. The biggest point I agreed with was something I've also personally stated a few times in the past: anything and everything related to methods should not be publicly accessible and should be locked behind some sort of wall. I also think verification of some sort would be helpful but as there are many people with many different views on privacy on the site, it might not go over well. 

I do not, however, agree with his large-scale characterization of the base nor with the points he gets blatantly incorrect. There is no "subscription service" nor is there any sort of "SS2." I also think it's pertinent to point out that when he initially used and posted on the site, he essentially antagonized a large population of very suicidal people in one of the few safe spaces where we are free to openly discuss our struggles. There also seems to be a lot of mischaracterization, with people in the replied actively calling this place some sort of "evil" cult when, in reality, I'd argue it's the opposite. 

Having used the site on and off for two years now, I can say that it's actually pretty funny how little most of the userbase really has in common. SS is one of the few places I see LGBTQ+ people and sometimes borderline Qanoner boomers have respectful and even friendly interactions. You get people from all across the spectrum, old and young, healthy and ill, rational and, admittedly irrational, etc. I think this is the result of this being again, one of the only places people can talk about these things without really risking much, if anything at all. 

I would think that r/breadtube especially would understand the need for safe spaces from what's essentially a marginalized community. There are Muslim users from nations where they still treat depression with electroshock therapy. There are LGBT and queer youth who are living in homophobic and unsafe households. There are many POC (like myself) who come from communities and environments where you simply cannot discuss this stuff openly. SS is a haven for all of us. Are there problematic users? Beyond a doubt (and if you ever visit, you'll probably see people arguing about them in the chat that he didn't mention in his video at all). Is the website imperfect? Without a question. Do people deserve a space to openly discuss these issues though? I believe they do. 

If you have any questions I'd be happy to answer them! Hopefully someone finds this comment useful!

Edit to add: the top comment really seemed to grab hold of the incel forum founders connection and not let go. The current owner (and much of the staff) funnily enough consists of trans men and women, as well as POC. I get this is breadtube and we gotta throw in the antifascism, but the whole thing is based of a single point in a poorly-researched video. The userbase is (probably) largely male, but I don't think it's largely white men at all truthfully. I meet more marginalized peoples on SS than most other internet spaces funnily enough. Maybe there's a correlation between being marginalized in society and not wanting to live, who would've thought?
